references.text: Moses turns again to the Lord with a prayer on behalf of the people and questions God's actions toward Israel.
Moses complains to the Lord about the burden of leading the people and asks why he was sent.
Joshua addresses the Lord with complaint and questions why God led the people into trouble.
Ruth asks 'why' in a similar way, an expression of wonder at unexpected treatment.
Job poses similar questions to God about why he is experiencing suffering, using the word 'why'.
Job asks God to explain why He acts this way toward him, similar to Moses' complaint.
The psalmist cries out 'why' to God in distress, an expression of lament resembling Moses' words.
The psalmist asks the Lord why He hides Himself and forgets the people's misery.
Jeremiah questions the Lord about justice, similar to Moses' address to God.
Jeremiah laments his calling and the burden of being a prophet, similar to Moses' frustration over his mission.
Habakkuk asks the Lord why He allows evil and suffering.
Moses' identical accusation that God acts 'evil' toward His people/servant in two different crises (persecution and burden) shows an ongoing theological struggle with God's methods of leadership.
Both verses show Moses as an intercessor asking God to stop His wrath against the people, but with different focus: on preceding suffering (5:22) versus subsequent judgment (32:11).

A theological contrast where Moses asks 'why do you act evil?' (5:22) while God asks 'how long will they not believe?' (14:11), illustrating the tension between the prophet's doubt and the people's unfaithfulness.
